summary.text: BASS aims to relate normal-gravity material flammability testing to flames burning in microgravity aboard the ISS, and to assess an inert gaseous extinguishing agent over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow.

fuels.text: Fabric samples of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass), Nomex fabric and Ultem.

geometry.text: Fabric samples in a 76 mm x 76 mm cross-section flow duct; other sample shapes included spheres and cylinders.

flow.text: Variable speed fan, airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s, in opposed or concurrent direction relative to flame spread.

measurements.text: Flame size, shape, color, spread rate and potential flame quenching, observed in top and edge profiles.

hardware.text: Microgravity Science Glovebox aboard the International Space Station.

claims.text: BASS aims to begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
BASS aims to assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
BASS hypothesizes that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity.

limitations.text: The metadata describes the objectives, hypothesis and approach but states no measured result, so no observation is recorded on this card.
Only PSI metadata was examined and no document text was processed.

modeling_resources.description: Experimental table for BASS listed in the PSI file inventory; flame size, shape, spread rate and quenching were collected according to the approach.

evidence.excerpt: Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem.
Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s.
The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric.
Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.
The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.
The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG).
Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching.
BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity
